newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Gaza nightlife flourishes under Arafat's rule.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gaza nightlife flourishes under Arafat's rule.

text.p: On a moonlit beach near President Yasser Arafat's office, Palestinians hypnotised by the undulations of a sultry, scantily clad figure bear witness to the new Gaza Strip.
Bellydancing and other nightlife are back in self-ruled Gaza thanks to a peace deal with Israel, a clampdown on Islamic militancy and the return of thousands of PLO officials.
Not everyone can afford the winds of cultural change in Gaza -- more than half of its one million Palestinians are jobless -- but it's little short of a revolution for those who can.
Gazans ascribe the strip's cultural makeover to Arafat's 1993 peace deal ending both the Israeli occupation and the "intifada," the Palestinian uprising.
Many say they feel released from the chains clamped on them by Israel's occupation and during the uprising by the militant Hamas movement and others.

"Before the intifada, life in Gaza was liberal. Women wore short skirts, restaurants served alcohol and women used to swim, and we had glamorous nightlife," said Um Yousef, a member of Gaza's wealthy elite.
"The self-made rules imposed by Hamas and PLO factions strangled us," added her husband.
Going to the beach was uncommon under Israeli occupation when curfews were imposed at sunset. Rich Gazans used to spend time in Israel or travel to neighbouring Egypt for fun.
Two years under PLO rule have changed all that.
Veiled religious women, who in the past walked out when belly dancers performed, now stay to watch.
At the beachfront Gaza Nights restaurant, revellers sing Arabic tunes and dance until dawn accompanied by a local band.
"The idea was to let people have a relaxing good time after a hard day's work. Every night more than 400 people arrive, and on weekends, more than 3,000," said manager Hashem Abul Nada.
"People lived a grim life under occupation, and now we are in the process of building a state, so we are transferring experiences of other nations to Gaza by hosting foreign bands."

Gazans said the return from exile of thousands of PLO officials and their families, who were exposed to liberal foreign lifestyles, has had a significant social effect on the West Bank and Gaza Strip.

Returnees, some of whom lived in Europe and Tunisia, felt suffocated by what they saw as the closed, uncultivated society they found in poverty stricken Gaza on their arrival in 1994, when Arafat's PLO took over under the peace deal with Israel.
Parties were at first confined to homes. But gradually people started to go to restaurants at the beach and reserved them for private parties.
Dozens of new hotels and restaurants were built along the beach, and some innkeepers began furtively serving alcohol to friends and customers.
Renowned Palestinian poets like Mahmoud Darwish became frequent guests at West Bank events. Thousands crowded festivals which moved from one Palestinian town to another.

An unlikely factor spurring liberalisation was a spate of Hamas suicide bombings that killed 59 people in Israel in February and March. Pressed by Israel, Arafat cracked down on the militants, marginalising them in Palestinian society.
The killing of 60 Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers in September clashes brought West Bank nightlife to a screeching halt but not in Gaza where it carried on as usual.
Gaza's elite have found special spots to unwind.
A man named Mohammed said Arafat's wife, Suha, takes guests to the new Windmill motel and restaurant across from her house.
"We danced all night during a dinner party at the Windmill, there was a band and a disc jockey and games. Prizes were television sets, a satellite dish and so on," Mohammed said.

"We have noticed there is a great reception for such dinner parties and the proof is that tickets are always sold out," said Basel Ilewa, owner of the Windmill. Tickets sell for $30, a prohibitive price for most people living in Gaza.
Ilewa said the peace process drew him and his brother back to Gaza from the United States.
"We came here to invest in our homeland, and the Palestinian Authority's presence helped us create the environment for implementing such projects."
Gaza Nights patron Zeinab Abdel-Rahim took another view.
"This is an opportunity to get people away from their daily concerns. It is a place for people to socialise outside of their homes and to meet new people," he said.
"It is better than spending nights at home watching boring television programmes."
